The morning light hit the kitchen counter at exactly 7:23, same as always, catching the rim of a coffee mug left there since Tuesday. Someone should move it. No one will. This is how houses become haunted—not by ghosts but by inertia, by the weight of small decisions deferred until they calcify into tradition. The mug stays. The light moves on.

I used to think memory worked like a filing cabinet. Now I believe it's more like a garden tended by a drunkard. Some things bloom wildly out of season; others, deliberately planted, never break soil. I can tell you the exact texture of a stranger's coat on a bus in 2007—wool, nubby, smelling of cigarettes and dog—but I walked past my own parked car last week, twice, searching for it like a tourist in my own neighborhood.

The body keeps its own counsel. My left knee knows rain before the sky does. There's a twinge in my shoulder that remembers a door I slammed in anger twenty years ago, the wood cracking, the hinge screaming, my hand somehow unhurt but never quite forgiven by the tendons. We think we're the protagonists of our stories, but mostly we're just the damage report.

There's a woman in Osaka who repairs broken pottery with gold. Kintsugi, she calls it, or someone does—I've never been to Osaka, never held gold lacquer in my hands, but I carry the idea of her like a stone in my pocket, smooth from handling. The philosophy is that breakage becomes part of the history, not something to disguise. I wonder what she'd make of me. I wonder if the gold would hold, or if I'm too many pieces, too many breaks, a mosaic that forgot it was ever a vase.

My grandmother spoke to her dead sister for eleven years. Not in séance, not in grief—just conversation, the way you might remark to a passenger about the scenery. "Martha would have liked this rain," she'd say, or "Martha never trusted that man." The sister died in 1958. The conversations continued until 2009, when my grandmother's own mind began to loosen from its moorings. I don't think she was crazy. I think she had developed a technology for loneliness, a workaround, an operating system patch. We all have them. The person who talks to their houseplants. The one who narrates their actions aloud when alone. The elaborate inner life of the commuter, the fantasy league, the imaginary argument perfected in the shower. We're not meant to be alone, and we are so often alone.

I read once that the human brain processes rejection in the same region that processes physical pain. Evolution couldn't be bothered to build separate systems. Heartbreak and broken femurs share neural real estate. This feels like a design flaw but maybe it's honesty. Maybe we've spent too long pretending these are different categories of suffering, the body and the heart, when they're just... suffering. The body and the heart. The mug and the counter. The light that keeps coming back, indifferent, beautiful, 7:23 again, again, again.

The coffee's cold now. I should move the mug.
